title: 3-Read Friday #13: Differentiated Questioning, Memory, and Chatbots
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #13 curates three posts spanning questioning technique, memory theory, and a skeptical take on classroom AI. Miss D Cox illustrates how rewording a retrieval question -- while keeping its content identical -- can shift how hard students actually have to think, giving teachers a tool for differentiating the "think ratio" once the "participation ratio" is already high. Blake Harvard proposes a simplified three-step model of memory -- Sense, Attend, Rehearse -- as an accessible entry point for teachers and students who don't have time to master the full technical literature on working memory and cognitive load. Dan Meyer offers a cautious counterpoint to AI hype in education, arguing chatbots are "neat" but not transformative for K-12 math instruction. Barton frames the set as a reminder that small design choices -- in questions, in mental models, in technology adoption -- carry outsized consequences for what students actually learn.
points: Rewording a retrieval question without changing its content can shift the "think ratio" -- how hard students actually have to think -- once the "participation ratio" is already secured through tools like mini-whiteboards.
Blake Harvard's Sense-Attend-Rehearse model compresses the technical literature on memory into a three-step framework simple enough to use as a classroom poster or a quick CPD session.
Dan Meyer's skepticism toward chatbots offers a useful counterweight to prevailing media narratives that generative AI will soon deliver high-quality, personalised education.

Barton's selections this week share a theme: precise, deliberate design choices -- in a question's wording, in a memory model, in how new technology is evaluated -- determine whether a tool actually helps students learn.

This blog by Miss Cox is so useful in this regard, illustrating how the wording of a question can be tweaked to impact the think ratio and thus tell us something different about our students’ depth of understanding.
In this post, Blake adds something before attention, namely sense.
I see this play out often when a child at the front of the class voices an answer, and a child at the back doesn't even have a sense that they have spoken.
It is all too easy to get carried away, believing chatbots will be all our students need to get high-quality, personalised education in the non-too-distant future.
Dan Meyer offers a sceptical, cautionary perspective, that is a useful counterpoint to prevailing views in the media.
